title: Reefs Under Pressure
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. The reef itself is built by tiny animals called polyps, which take calcium from seawater and deposit it as a hard skeleton. Over thousands of years, countless generations of polyps build on the skeletons of their predecessors, creating structures large enough to be seen from space.

Reefs take three main forms, a classification described by Charles Darwin in the 1840s. A fringing reef grows directly from the shore, with little or no water between it and the land. A barrier reef lies farther out, separated from the coast by a deep channel or lagoon; the best known runs for more than two thousand kilometres along the Australian coast. An atoll is a ring of coral surrounding a lagoon, with no land at its centre. Darwin proposed that an atoll forms when a volcanic island with a fringing reef slowly sinks while the coral continues to grow upwards, and later research largely confirmed his idea.

Corals depend on a partnership. Inside the tissues of each polyp live microscopic algae that supply most of its energy and give the reef its colour. When the water becomes too warm, the polyps expel the algae and the coral turns white, a process known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but without its partner it begins to starve, and if the heat lasts for more than a few weeks it usually dies. Severe bleaching events, once rare, have become frequent enough that some reefs have no time to recover between them.

Heat is not the only danger. Run-off from farmland carries fertiliser to the sea, where it feeds seaweed that smothers coral. Fishing with explosives destroys the structure of the reef, and the overfishing of parrotfish, which graze on algae, allows seaweed to spread. Cyclones and outbreaks of the crown-of-thorns starfish, which feeds on coral, cause further damage, although reefs have always recovered from such natural events when left alone. It is the combination of pressures that now worries scientists, since a reef weakened by pollution recovers far more slowly from a storm.

The best-known response is coral gardening. Fragments are broken from healthy colonies, grown on frames in underwater nurseries until they are large enough, and then attached to damaged reef with cement or clips. Dr Maria Okafor's team has reported that fragments survive more often when they are attached in groups than when they are planted singly, probably because neighbours shelter one another from strong currents. In several projects, restored patches have attracted fish within months, and some have begun to spawn naturally.

Professor Daniel Reyes does not want gardening abandoned, but he believes that its importance is often exaggerated. A planted coral will bleach and die just as surely as a wild one if the water stays too warm, he points out, and the cost of restoring a single hectare is very high. Because only a few fast-growing species are normally planted, a restored reef also tends to have less variety than the original. In his view, the first priority must be to cut greenhouse gas emissions and to improve the quality of coastal water.

A newer idea is to look for corals that can tolerate heat. Some colonies growing in naturally hot lagoons survive temperatures that kill their neighbours elsewhere, and researchers have begun to breed them, or to move them to cooler reefs. So far this has been tried only in small trials, and nobody yet knows whether such corals will be able to cope with other threats, such as disease. Supporters of gardening argue that it should continue regardless, because it buys time while longer-term solutions are developed.
